title: TWO DESPERATE MOTHERS MADE A HORRIFYING AGREEMENT DURING THE SIEGE OF SAMARIA
paragraphs: TWO DESPERATE MOTHERS MADE A HORRIFYING AGREEMENT DURING THE SIEGE OF SAMARIA

One mother kept her terrible promise. The other hid her son. But buried inside one of the Bible’s darkest stories is a warning about what happens when desperation replaces trust in God—and a breathtaking picture of the God who can bring abundance to a city that has reached the end of itself.
There are Bible stories we love to put on walls.
David facing Goliath.
Daniel among the lions.
Moses before the Red Sea.
Jesus calming the storm.
And then there are passages like this one.
Passages we read once...
and wish we had not seen.
Because 2 Kings 6 takes us inside a starving city and introduces us to two mothers who had become so desperate that they made an agreement almost impossible to comprehend.
One of their children would die today.
The other would die tomorrow.
They would eat them.
And one mother actually kept her side of the agreement.
Read that again slowly.
Not because the horror should entertain us.
Because Scripture refuses to lie about how far human suffering and rebellion can descend.
Samaria was under siege.
Ben-hadad, king of Aram, had surrounded the city. Nothing was getting through. Food disappeared. Prices became grotesque. Hunger began stripping away the normal rhythms of civilization.
The Hebrew text says:
וַיְהִי רָעָב גָּדוֹל בְּשֹׁמְרוֹן
Vayehi ra'av gadol beShomron.
“And there was a great famine in Samaria.”
That word רָעָב — ra'av means famine, hunger.
But by the time the biblical narrator brings us to these two women, “hunger” almost feels too small a word.
A donkey's head had become extraordinarily expensive. Even something translated as “dove's dung”—whose precise identification has been debated—was being sold at a desperate price.
This wasn't skipping dinner.
This wasn't an empty refrigerator.
This was civilization collapsing one stomach at a time.
Then the king of Israel was walking along the city wall when a woman screamed to him for help.
“Help me, my lord the king!”
Imagine her voice.
Maybe cracked from dehydration.
Maybe trembling.
Maybe furious.
Maybe carrying a grief so deep she didn't even know how to cry anymore.
The king's response was revealing:
“If the LORD does not help you, where can I find help for you?”
He had no grain.
No wine.
No solution.
A king was standing above a starving woman wearing a crown that could not save her.
And there is something painfully familiar about that.
We keep discovering things we thought could save us...
until the siege comes.
Money feels powerful until money cannot fix what is broken.
Influence feels powerful until influence cannot quiet your conscience.
Pleasure feels powerful until you are alone after midnight and the emptiness returns.
People feel powerful until the person you built your identity around walks away.
Religion can even become something we hide behind until suffering tears open the costume and reveals whether we actually know God.
The king asked the woman what was wrong.
And then came the sentence that must have frozen him where he stood.
She explained that another woman had proposed an agreement:
אֶת־בְּנֵךְ וְנֹאכְלֶנּוּ הַיּוֹם וְאֶת־בְּנִי נֹאכַל מָחָר
In context:
“Your son... we will eat him today, and my son we will eat tomorrow.”
Then she continued.
וַנְּבַשֵּׁל אֶת־בְּנִי וַנֹּאכְלֵהוּ
Vannevashel et-beni vannokhelehu.
“We boiled my son and ate him.”
There are sentences in Scripture that should never become ordinary to us.
This is one of them.
A mother had once carried that little boy inside her.
She had felt him move.
She had given birth to him.
Perhaps she had held him through fever.
Perhaps she knew exactly how he sounded when he laughed.
Perhaps she had watched him sleep.
And somehow starvation had brought her to a place where the child she once fed from her own body became food for hers.
Then came the next day.
She went to the other mother.
It was time for the second woman to fulfill her promise.
But the text says:
וַתַּחְבִּא אֶת־בְּנָהּ
Vattachbi et-benah.
“She hid her son.”
And suddenly the first mother was standing before the king demanding justice.
Think about how broken everything had become.
The complaint wasn't simply, “My child is dead.”
Her grievance was essentially:
“I kept the agreement. She didn't.”
That is how distorted suffering can make the human heart.
And before we stand safely outside this story and condemn these women as monsters, we should notice what Scripture is doing.
The Bible had warned Israel that covenant rebellion could eventually bring siege conditions of precisely this horrifying kind.
Deuteronomy 28:53 warned of a time when, under siege and distress, people would eat “the fruit of your womb.”
The Hebrew is devastating:
וְאָכַלְתָּ פְרִי־בִטְנְךָ
Ve'akhaltā peri-vitnekha.
“You shall eat the fruit of your womb.”
Leviticus 26:29 likewise warned:
וַאֲכַלְתֶּם בְּשַׂר בְּנֵיכֶם וּבְשַׂר בְּנֹתֵיכֶם
“You shall eat the flesh of your sons and the flesh of your daughters.”
This does not make the women's actions morally good.
It makes the scene even more terrifying.
The covenant warnings were no longer distant words.
The warning had walked into Samaria.
The warning had entered someone's kitchen.
The warning had become a mother's testimony before the king.
Sin always promises freedom before revealing the chains.
That is still how it works.
Nobody wakes up planning to destroy everything precious.
Compromise usually arrives quietly.
Just this once.
Nobody will know.
You deserve this.
You can stop whenever you want.
God understands.
Tomorrow you'll repent.
And tomorrow becomes next month.
Next month becomes next year.
The secret becomes a habit.
The habit becomes a master.
And eventually you look around at the wreckage and wonder:
“How did I get here?”
Maybe your siege doesn't look like Samaria.
Maybe nobody sees yours at all.
Maybe your siege happens when the bedroom door closes.
Maybe it's pornography you promised Jesus you would stop watching.
Maybe bitterness toward somebody has lived inside you so long that hatred now feels justified.
Maybe you smile at church while privately wondering whether you still believe anything you sing.
Maybe your marriage looks alive publicly and feels dead privately.
Maybe success has become your god.
Maybe you're exhausted from pretending.
Maybe there is something hidden on your phone, in your relationship, in your bank statements, in your thoughts, or inside your heart that you desperately hope nobody ever discovers.
And somewhere along the way, you started making agreements with desperation.
“I'll compromise this once.”
“I'll hide this.”
“I'll become this person just to survive.”
“I'll deal with God later.”
Listen carefully.
The terrifying lesson of Samaria is not merely that desperate people can do unimaginable things.
It is that when humanity moves farther and farther from God, things we once thought impossible can eventually become negotiable.
But the story does not end with the mothers.
Thank God.
Because while Samaria was collapsing, God was not absent.
The king tore his clothes when he heard the woman's story.
Underneath his royal garments was sackcloth.
He was grieving.
But grief is not necessarily repentance.
Instead of humbling himself before God, the king turned his rage toward Elisha.
He wanted the prophet dead.
That is another frightening possibility.
Sometimes when God's Word exposes us, we would rather attack the messenger than surrender to the message.
We blame the church.
We blame our spouse.
We blame our childhood.
We blame Christians who disappointed us.
We blame circumstances.
Sometimes we even blame God.
Anything except saying the words that heaven is waiting to hear:
“Lord... I have sinned.”
Yet right there, when everything looked irrecoverable, Elisha announced something outrageous.
“Listen to the word of the LORD.”
Tomorrow...
food.
Tomorrow...
abundance.
Tomorrow...
the market that had been destroyed by famine would change.
Not eventually.
Not after a military campaign lasting six months.
Tomorrow.
One royal officer essentially laughed at the possibility.
Even if God opened windows in heaven, could something like that happen?
He could see the siege.
He could calculate the food shortage.
He could measure the impossibility.
What he could not calculate was God.
And while Samaria slept hungry, something was happening outside the walls.
Four marginalized men went toward the Aramean camp expecting that they might die.
Instead, they discovered something unbelievable.
The camp was abandoned.
Scripture tells us that the Lord had caused the Aramean army to hear the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army.
They panicked.
They fled.
They left food behind.
They left possessions behind.
They left everything.
Samaria thought salvation required an army.
God used a sound.
The starving city thought the enemy was still surrounding them.
The enemy had already run away.
Don't miss that.
There were people inside Samaria starving beside a provision they did not yet know existed.
And perhaps somebody reading this feels exactly like that spiritually.
You think your sin has the final word.
You think what you did is too ugly.
You think your addiction has owned you too long.
You think your marriage has gone too far.
You think God is tired of hearing you repent.
You think the years you wasted have permanently disqualified you.
You think the scandal became your identity.
But the Gospel announces something greater than self-improvement.
Jesus Christ entered our famine.
He entered our broken world.
He came to sinners who could not rescue themselves.
He lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And on the third day...
the tomb was empty.
Christianity is not the announcement that bad people can polish themselves until God tolerates them.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Grace does not pretend sin is harmless.
The cross proves exactly the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with God required what we could never provide for ourselves.
Yet God's love is so astonishing that Christ came willingly.
That is why the Gospel can look directly at your worst chapter without looking away.
The cross has already seen scandal.
Peter denied Jesus.
A thief died beside Him.
Paul had persecuted Christians.
The woman caught in adultery was dragged into public shame.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
Again and again, Jesus met people at places they probably wished could be erased from their stories.
And He did not call darkness light.
He called sinners to repentance...
and offered grace.
That distinction matters.
Grace is not Jesus saying, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
Grace is Jesus calling us out of the grave.
Repentance is not payment for salvation.
We could never pay.
It is the turning of the sinner toward the Savior who alone can save.
The mothers of Samaria show us where human desperation can descend.
The empty Aramean camp shows us how quickly God can overturn circumstances.
But the cross shows us something infinitely greater:
what God has done about humanity's deepest siege.
Sin.
Guilt.
Judgment.
Death.
The Gospel does not promise that following Jesus means every earthly famine disappears tomorrow.
Christians suffer.
Christians grieve.
Christians bury people they love.
Christians walk through seasons when heaven seems painfully quiet.
So don't turn 2 Kings 7 into a formula saying every crisis will disappear within twenty-four hours.
That isn't what the text promises us.
What Scripture gives us is better than a formula.
It gives us God.
A God whose Word remains true when circumstances scream otherwise.
A God who is not defeated by impossible situations.
And ultimately, a Savior whose resurrection guarantees that sin and death will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
Maybe that is why this disturbing story has found you today.
Not so you can stare at two desperate mothers from thousands of years ago.
But so you will ask what desperation has been doing inside you.
What have you been feeding that is slowly consuming what you love?
What compromise have you renamed “survival”?
What sin have you protected because surrender feels too expensive?
What have you hidden?
Who have you blamed?
How long have you been standing behind the walls of your own Samaria, starving spiritually while refusing to come home to God?
You do not need another disguise.
You need Jesus.
Not religious performance.
Jesus.
Not another promise that you'll fix yourself next Monday.
Jesus.
Not another carefully edited Christian image.
Jesus.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is mercy for the ashamed.
There is cleansing for the guilty.
There is restoration for the broken.
There is a new identity stronger than the worst thing you have ever done.
Your scandal does not become good.
Grace does something better.
Grace refuses to let the scandal have the final sentence.
That is why we keep saying it:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the ugly pages never happened.
But by taking ruined people and making them trophies of mercy.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a spiritual speech. Just be honest.
Somebody scrolling beneath this article may desperately need evidence that God still restores broken lives.
Don't underestimate what your testimony can do in another person's midnight.
And don't keep this article trapped on this page.
Not as a superstition. Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. Salvation is by grace; a Facebook share cannot purchase it.
Supporting a ministry does not make God love you more.
Sharing does not earn heaven.
Jesus purchased salvation—not us.
But when Christ has given us good news, we can gladly help carry that good news to others.
If Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, stay close.
Because there may come a night when you need to remember that the situation screaming “finished” is not sovereign.
God is.
And before you leave, remember the two mothers.
Remember the starving city.
Remember the abandoned enemy camp.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Samaria's darkest night was not proof that God had ceased to be God.
And your darkest chapter does not possess the authority to write the ending of your story.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Bring the guilt.
Bring the addiction.
Bring the anger.
Bring the shame.
Bring the shattered marriage.
Bring the questions.
Bring the years you wasted.
Bring the secret you wish you could erase.
Bring yourself.
Not to an algorithm.
Not to a ministry.
Not to Gospel Warrior.
Bring yourself to Jesus Christ.
It is pointing another human soul toward the Savior.
The chapter that makes you ashamed to tell your story may become the very place where people someday see how fiercely Christ's grace pursued you.
